utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: This sitting is resumed. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case IT-94-1-A-R77, the Prosecutor versus Dusko Tadic in a matter concerning allegations against prior counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The next witness is not a protected witness, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, the next witness is not a protected witness. It is Michail Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you have him called into court, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been done already, Your Honour. He's been called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, I believe you are no stranger to this setting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Will you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, we have gone over the part about your name. Your name is Michail Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you state the date and place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. I'm born on the 10th of January, 1945, in The Hague, The Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Your profession is that of an attorney?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you made a statement, a written statement, dated 6 April 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, may the witness be shown the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement will be marked Exhibit 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is that your statement, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: When you made it, the contents were true and correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You still say so today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Then unless there are any objections, this statement is admitted, and it has been marked, as the Registrar suggested, 35. Mr. Wladimiroff, will you kindly take some questions from Mr. Abell, who is counsel for an interested party, Mr Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, I'm not going to take you in detail right through the statement that you have made and which is now Exhibit 35, because you have adopted it as being the truth in relation to your dealings with this case and Mr. Vujin. Firstly, that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'd like to just ask, if you can, to assist with one or two aspects of your statement, please. If we go to paragraph 4 of your statement, you mention -- five lines down, you say this: "During my assignment on the case, the Registrar never assigned Mr. Vujin as co-counsel to Mr Tadic."

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I've never been aware of any assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: As far as you were aware during your time when you were assigned by the ICTY to represent Mr Tadic, was Mr. Vujin, so far as you were aware, ever receiving any payment for his assistance from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not as far as I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Were you aware of any means by which Mr. Vujin was receiving any payment in relation to his work; any fees, that is, in relation to his work on the case?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not as far as I was aware. As I mentioned in this statement, I paid for travel expenses on occasions, but I've never been aware of any payments in terms of fees paid to Mr. Vujin by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. From your statement, he worked in the case whilst you were in it for many months, did he not?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. Essentially one year; April '95 up to April '96, if I'm right in dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. You say, in paragraph 6, that witness statements that Mr. Vujin presented to you were of very poor quality, "in that none of them provided any information that I was looking for." Again on the same topic, in paragraph 7 on page 3, third line down, you said that you explained to Mr. Vujin again "what I was looking for by way of evidence; that is, full and detailed statements of people who had direct knowledge of the movements of Mr Tadic at the material time, and no statements of people who could only testify about his," that is, Mr Tadic's "character. Despite this, I later received more statements which were of no use to the Defence." That's true, is it?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Can you think of any really useful statement that came from Mr. Vujin or from the two investigators whom he suggested you employed, Mr. Kostic and Mr. Drazic; can you think of any really useful statement that was provided either by Mr. Vujin or by his two investigators during your time in the case, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Talking about Mr. Kostic and Drazic, I do remember statements that were useful -- there were only a few, but there were. I can't remember any name, but I do remember that some of them were useful indeed. And as far as Mr. Vujin is concerned, I can't remember any specific statement, because as far as I remember, he did not sign any statements, or I'm not aware who was the author of -- who made up the note about the interview. So I can't answer that last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well. Did you consider that Mr. Vujin, given where he lived and given that there were two investigators, Mr. Kostic and Mr. Drazic, did you consider that Mr. Vujin ought to have been in a more advantageous position than you to get at the evidence, to get at the facts and to get the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In my assumption, in 1995, yes. In 1996, I got this feeling of having ties with people which were not in the benefit of the Tadic case in terms of being familiar with them. And then it became extremely difficult for me to understand what he could or what he could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: When you say "having ties with people," who did you have the feeling was having ties with people, to use your phrase, which were not in the benefit of the Tadic case?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, he knew people -- again, it's very difficult for me now to remember names, but he knew people who were in power in those days in the Republika Srpska as well as in Yugoslavia. And again, I feel sorry not being able to provide you with any name, but it's a general feeling of feeling uncomfortable about his knowledge, his ties, as I described it, with people who are in power. So it became, as I said, extremely difficult, because I was not there, but I learned about these ties. I remember, for example, (redacted) (redacted) telling me about this. This is knowledge I pass to you I have not been able to check myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Just so that we know who you're talking about, are you talking about somebody by the name of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I couldn't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Don't worry. And try to remember what he said to you about this, as best you can, the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: At the beginning he was -- and then I'm referring to 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: -- he was boasting about the ties of Mr. Vujin with the authorities. Later on, in 1996, up to March, because then I fell ill -- and later on I saw him again, but then we didn't discuss that matter because Vujin was already exited -- at the beginning of 1996, he was complaining about it, and that's what I remember. I can't pass to you any contents of that complaint, but it supported my feeling of feeling uncomfortable about these ties. And I tried to express that in the statement by saying that we did not want to confront Mr. Vujin; we simply tried to sideline him, not to have any clash. Because we were not able to understand what these ties were, so we didn't want to run any risk in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Does it come to this: You were concerned that if there was a confrontation with Mr. Vujin, that that could do damage to the Defence case for Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's what we thought. It never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: It never came to a confrontation, as such?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Now, can I please go to paragraph 8 of your statement, where you refer to September of 1995, when you returned to Bosnia. You say that on one occasion whilst you were there, you travelled by bus to Banja Luka with your interpreter to test whether you could cross the border without the assistance of Mr. Vujin, and he arrived the next day with his own car. Firstly, were you able to cross the border without the assistance of Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: "He arrived the next day with his own car. We did some interviews together. On one occasion which I remember very clearly, he interrupted a witness I was interviewing and told the witness what to say. My interpreter told the witness simply to answer my questions and to ignore Mr. Vujin. He did not like this, and he verbally abused her. This was the first very clear example of Mr. Vujin trying to interfere with the evidence a witness could give by telling the interviewee how to answer a question." Firstly, that's a true recollection of the events, is it?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is. It is on videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Right. And I'm going to ask if we can see, in just a moment, a piece of video, and see if it is the incident you're speaking of or not. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Was there a video or was there a programme on Dutch television in relation to the Tadic case which featured you to some extent, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Is that the programme that you are speaking of?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And let me see if we have identified or not identified the correct passage in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, there should be with the Court a transcript of certain sections of this video recording, which I believe the clerk has, which I have down as Exhibit 8A, [Realtime transcript read in error 8PA] because at one point it was shown briefly on an earlier occasion when we were sitting in the upstairs court, Court 3. I don't know whether the Court has copies or whether they could be handed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What exhibit is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Well, I have on the top of mine Exhibit 8A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Because the transcript says 8PA. 8A?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We'll have to see if the Registrar has-- yes. Would you require the video to be played?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. It should be set up in the correct position, if, from what I did this morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Have the arrangements been made, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: It should be in the video booth, Your Honour. It may be of assistance if Your Honours have the translation first of all, and we'll find out from Mr. Vujin if this is the incident he recollects or not.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Before we move on to the actual recording, I'd like to tell you that I do not have Exhibit 8A. What I suggest to you is that we give a number for the videotape; it will be Exhibit 36, and the transcript of that cassette will be Exhibit 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No objections; it is so ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Just before it's played, Mr. Wladimiroff, can you assist us as to approximately when this programme, of which we are going to see a recording of excerpts, was made?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I guess, because I certainly can't give you exact dates, in the beginning of '97, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, now I'm going to ask that the excerpt from the video at 1531 be played, please. If you watch it with us, Mr. Wladimiroff, once it's over, tell us if this is the passage you are speaking of. May I take a seat, Your Honours, while this is played?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Doesn't matter. This is the lawyer from Holland. He wants to ask you a few questions, that you brought coffee here and so on. Did you? Yes. I would take it out and get coffee for everyone, and for Dusko Tadic, too. I couldn't care less what he's going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Firstly, is that the passage -- is that the incident that you are recollecting in the tape, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm just wondering. No disrespect of Madam Interpreter who was interpreting, but it may be easier -- we have a transcript. May I suggest that we play it again, but without Madam Interpreter giving an interpretation, and then we can hear what's been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I have a difficulty, and I don't know if it is shared by colleagues on the Bench. The interpretation seemed to be a truncated form of the version which appears in print. I'm not sure whether my impression is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Does Your Honour mean the verbal interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. We didn't have the transcript, so we didn't know what we were supposed to do, whether to translate from what we heard or not. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: We quite understand that. The suggestion I'm going to make is I simply ask Mr. Wladimiroff to identify the relevant people, and then perhaps if Your Honours agree, we'll play that excerpt again without Madam Interpreter interpreting verbally, and we can follow, if we wish, on the transcript, which I understand translates both Dutch and B/C/S as and when necessary. However, I believe this is all in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I better hear the parties on that, because I think what the Court would be interested in is to learn, through the interpreters, what exactly was being said in the video clip. We have no assurance that the typed document presented to us in fact reflects what is being said in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: May I make two points on that? I entirely understand. I understand that the Court, in fact, translated these excerpts on an earlier occasion. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Secondly, it may be that Your Honours will be reassured as to the accuracy of this translation if a copy of it is given to Madam Interpreter, and she can perhaps follow it through in the booth while it's being played again, if that is a satisfactory course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: On this basis, that what we are to be guided by is the interpretation we receive from the booth. The booth can undoubtedly look also at this typed script to check, against the typed script, the accuracy of what they are interpreting. But I think we would want to know the interpretation placed by the booth on what is now being said by the parties in the video clip which we will now be seeing or have now seen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the booths please be given copies of that transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Just whilst that documentation is being handed to the interpreter, could I, Mr. Wladimiroff -- if you need to see it to remind yourself, do so, but could we just, Your Honour, identify the personnel we see on the video? There is yourself in, if I may put it, a light-coloured jacket in the video; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin we can recognise, obviously. There is a fair-haired lady with short, fair hair. Was that an interpreter who was with you?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: There is a dark-haired lady who appears to be the person which you are trying to interview?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Just remind us where it was again.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Outside of Prijedor, as far as I remember well, at a checkpoint near the road -- it was a checkpoint at the road, and we interviewed a farmer's wife near that checkpoint at her farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What information were you hoping to elicit or discover from interviewing her?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: First, whether she had seen Mr. Tadic at the material time and whether she could substantiate that by more detail; dates, type of days in the week, whom he was with, whether she was familiar with those others who were also there, where he slept, because I was told there was a house near that checkpoint where those who were on guard could sleep; whether she would serve them coffee or provide them with food, such kind of details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Perhaps now would be an appropriate moment to replay it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Perhaps simply listening to what the video itself says.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Do the interpreters interpret verbally or just follow the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Judges would like you to interpret for them what you will be hearing on the video. You may use the transcript to check the accuracy of your interpretation, if you so wish. But what we want to know is the interpretation which you now place on what is being said in the video. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] It doesn't matter. This is the lawyer from Holland. He was wondering whether he could ask you a couple of questions. He's my husband. He can. He can also. We were told that the gentleman that you -- well, that you took them coffee and so on. Yes. I gave them as much coffee as I had. I would take it out to them here. But you took the kit to Dusko Tadic as well? Yes, yes. He was out there too. Uh-huh, yes. I know well what he doesn't say. I couldn't care less. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, is there some more to be played?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. My only concern is that there is, on the transcript, a little more translated than we heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: This indeed tallies with my initial observation, and that is why I suggested that we should see the tape again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Could we just see the next part, just to see if there's more after this in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would like to say that whoever was listening to the tape must have listened to it more carefully and in greater detail and several times over to have got everything down in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. We understand that. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that there is less in what the interpreters told us here, that there is less that is being said, especially when Vujin said something, because we believe that the written translation -- that the transcript we received is absolutely accurate, that it contains everything that is contained in Exhibit 35. Especially, I do not see at all the words, "I want to say what I want," because Mr. Vujin said that towards the end, before he said, "I don't care about what he has to say," later. He believed that Mr. Vujin said the words that can be found in the translation, in the translated transcript in English, the one we have received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, perhaps we could listen to you further in the course of your summation at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: If I understand Mr. Domazet correctly, he is admitting, on behalf of his client, Mr. Vujin, that the written transcript which the Court prepared is an accurate one. That is the admission which is being made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is that the position of all parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did receive this transcript. It's our understanding that it was completed by the translation section at the Tribunal. We certainly have no doubt that they listened very carefully to the tape, as often as they needed to, and gave an accurate translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, the Court receives the written translation, by consent of parties, as an accurate rendition of what was, in fact, said in the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful. May I make the suggestion I made a little earlier, which is this: that the interpreter now doesn't interpret verbally, that now we know that this is an accurate translation by consent of all the parties, that we have a translation in front of us and merely listen to the voices on the video, simply so we get a flavour of the sounds that are being made? That would be my application: we play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You consider that is necessary, that we should run the tape a third time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Simply so -- because all we've heard so far is the interpreter's translation, and one can't really hear the voices very well on the actual tape. That's all it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Could that please be done, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We're not getting the image on the computer before us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want both images -- the image and the sound, or do you want the image and no interpretation, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Image and sound from the video, no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is what I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: We can see there, can't we, that the interpreter in the field, the lady with the short, fair hair, appears to be turning to Mr. Vujin, and as we can see from the transcript, effectively saying, "Hang on, I won't ask questions until -- unless he tells me to," referring to you, Mr. Wladimiroff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right. I note, however, that I would have only been aware of the translation in Dutch as was accessible to me by the Dutch subtitles, so the last page of the three pages you gave to me were familiar to me. I have never heard it in so detail as I've done now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. Again, it may be too obvious to say, but we should have it in evidence. It looks as if on that occasion there was a cameraman literally at your and Mr. Vujin's elbow whilst this conversation was going on?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. On that occasion, that was the case, and the procedure was first to select who would have any direct knowledge and then later on to do the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. Was that video there for the purposes of making a documentary or for the purposes of giving you a video recording of any useful leads you might come across during your investigation?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There was a third purpose too. The first two were right. The third purpose was to provide a form of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I see. Security because you're making investigations in the field?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I see. Now, you say in your paragraph that you regarded what Mr. Vujin did on that occasion as the first very clear example -- I'm looking at the last three lines, the last sentence of paragraph 8 of your statement. This was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Abell. Mr. Wladimiroff, would you like to go back to your reference to one of the purposes of the camera arrangement was to give you a form of security? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As long as you are in the field with a camera team, your risk of being arrested are less. That's what I assumed in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I also add to the Court, just to be precise on this matter, the condition of the cameraman being there was that it could only be broadcasted if I agreed to what would be broadcast or not after the verdict and the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well. You say that this was the first very clear example of Mr. Vujin trying to interfere with the evidence a witness could give by telling the interviewee how to answer a question. Firstly, is that how you regarded that incident that we've just seen on the video?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Secondly, on that particular occasion, and indeed on all occasions when you were in the field with Mr. Vujin, who was the person who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You were lead counsel, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Although one tries to be as collegial as one can be, but yes, I was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. And thirdly, were there other examples, as your investigation on behalf of Dusko Tadic, your then-client, went on, were there other examples that you witnessed of Mr. Vujin seeking to interfere with evidence by telling the interviewee how to answer a question, or by some other means?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, again, it's very difficult to give further detailed examples. It's more or less a pattern of -- a tendency with him to react to what witnesses say, either to correct them or to advise them. So as a patron, I do remember that I taught him -- "Please, let me ask the questions; don't interfere. I would rather prefer, myself, having the evidence coming in freshly from the witness and not having you tell the witness what to tell." It's not one or more specific occasions I can pass to by giving you names or dates. It's more or less a pattern. It happened on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And again, presumably, if and when Mr. Vujin interrupted, it would be in his own language?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. So I may have missed more occasions than I'm aware of, but sometimes my -- I -- well, I heard him talking, of course, and then I asked my interpreter what he was saying, and I would frankly say, without making any problem, "I would rather prefer to do it myself."

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. Were you concerned about what the interpreter was telling you was being asked by Mr. Vujin on these other occasions?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, it grew. At the beginning, I regarded it as his willingness to (indiscernible) and well done. Later on, I understood that it was a habit. And then, much more later, one understands that he was more or less directing witnesses, and then I got this feeling of -- this is not right; he is manipulating here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. And you've obviously been a lawyer of many years' standing, which this Court don't need to be told; they know. You use a stronger word in paragraph 9 of your statement: "There were further instances of this sort of behaviour which, it became apparent, could only be described as manipulations of the witness." No doubt you considered carefully before you put that sentence in your declaration, Mr. Wladimiroff; is that what you thought --

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: At the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: By the end?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, at the end, that's -- if you look back, that's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: It may be obvious, but did that situation cause you grave concern?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It worried me so much that later on, when the others made their own observations -- and I'm referring to Mr. Orie, co-counsel, and Mr. Kay, co-counsel -- that they really urged me -- I was more -- I was more willing to let it go and try to correct things myself, but they were very strong in their views, we should get rid of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And putting it bluntly, because they considered his conduct to be, frankly, improper?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. Now, can you help me, please, with this: Mr. Stephen Kay is a barrister from England?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Since his involvement in the Tadic case, it's within your knowledge that he has been appointed as Queen's Counsel in England?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Later on, since his involvement?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And Mr. Orie, just so that we have it in evidence, he --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpreting? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, he's a lawyer from where?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: He was partner in my firm, and now he is a judge in the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: He's now a judge, but what sort of seniority, if I can put it in that way? In England we call it "when was he called"; in other words, when was he admitted as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. First he was a senior researcher at the University of Leiden, and in 1980 he became a partner in our law firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you assist me about this, please. I think you told us earlier -- you used the phrase "sideline." You decided to try to "sideline" Mr. Vujin with the investigations, and I think you said earlier that you were anxious to avoid a confrontation. Do you mean that if he had been told point blank that he was off the case, if I can put it that way, because his behaviour was unacceptable to the other lawyers, were you concerned what the repercussions might be to the Tadic defence?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We could only guess, but since we had all that problems with authorities who were not willing to cooperate with us, we felt that if we would make him a declared enemy, and since he had these specified ties with the authorities, we were convinced that it would not be in the benefit of Mr. Tadic, so we have chosen for the policy of -- just let it fade away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to deal, please, with what you say in paragraph 14. Dealing now with Mr. Drljaca, the then-chief of police at Prijedor police station, did you have some dealings with Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I have met with Mr. Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What -- and indeed you deal with it to some extent in paragraph 10, but I'm trying to, as it were, be as brief as I can in asking you to expand on your statement -- what was your assessment of the attitude of that gentleman, Mr. Drljaca, to the investigation of people charged with committing war crimes?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It would be an understatement to say that he was not amused. In fact, he was the -- as far as I remember, the man in absolute power in that area in those days. He considered my appearance in the area as interfering with domestic affairs I had nothing to do with. He had very strong views on the Tribunal, in terms of they should not be here; they should not interfere; they should not send people. In sum, he did everything he could to block what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And again, put in simple terms, were you seeking to establish evidence to support Mr. Tadic's contention that he was an innocent man?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I was looking for evidence that could substantiate his claim that he was elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. And even if that involved bringing up -- bringing in the names of other people who may have been involved?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, to put it very bluntly, I'm not concerned with the interest of other people. I'm only concerned with the interests of Mr. Tadic. So I was looking for those people who could supply me with relevant evidence, whatever the consequences for themselves could be. If those consequences were within the reach of the authority of the Tribunal to protect them, I would advise the Tribunal to protect them within the possibility of the Tribunal. That's all I could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm sure we're all familiar with the concept. You're representing your client; you're going to do everything you can to present his case in its best possible light?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: If establishing that he was elsewhere involves other names being mentioned and other people possibly being implicated, that's not your concern; your concern is representing your client?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is this: Mr. Drljaca, in your assessment from your dealings with him, was he at all sympathetic to the idea of other people's names being dragged into it and possibly implicated in war crimes?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, I would say obviously, but not specifically -- he did not specifically say that, but his whole attitude was, "Don't interfere in my reign here." He acted like the local king. So a part of that attitude was that he didn't want me to meddle in anything that happened there, whatever it was. He simply didn't want me to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, was it obvious from Mr. Vujin's position that he realised what Mr. Drljaca's attitude was in relation to war crimes investigations?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I took it that he was more familiar with the situation there and what has happened in terms of what -- where Mr. Drljaca came from, as he travelled more in the area than I did. I took it for granted that he knew exactly who Mr. Drljaca was. I had to learn the man; he knew already who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, as you say in paragraph 10, Mr. Vujin had seen Mr. Drljaca before you, I think in September 1995, and indeed had reported to you that Mr. Drljaca didn't want to see you?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I was waiting outside the police station with, I think, one of the brothers of Mr. Tadic, because Mr. Drljaca did not want to see me. That's what I had been told. Then Mr. Vujin went into the police station. He talked to Mr. Drljaca -- at least, that was told to me. Now, later on he came back, and I was told that Mr. Drljaca didn't want to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: So if I can put it this way, Mr. Vujin's meeting with Mr. Drljaca, did it open any doors for you, or, put bluntly, did it close some doors in your face?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It did not open the door. And later on, I was a little bit surprised that the next time I was there, I had this easy access to Mr. Drljaca. So, jumping to conclusions, I would say why didn't that happen in September?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: But in terms of getting hold of witnesses, did Mr. Vujin's visit with Mr. Drljaca open doors or not?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say what could have happened if something had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I won't ask you to speculate, then.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on paragraph 14. A list of Defence witnesses had been prepared, had it not --

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- by the Defence team: by yourself, Mr. Kay, and Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right. I prepared the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, and these were potential Defence witnesses, people whom, in your estimation, on Mr. Tadic's instructions and from your investigations, could be useful people to interview --

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- and possibly to call to support Mr. Tadic's defence at his trial?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you want Mr. Drljaca to see that document?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You tell us there that you discovered, when you went to the Prijedor police station in -- I believe it would have been approximately April of '96, thereabouts, that you saw that list on Mr. Drljaca's desk.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I don't think it was April, because at that time I was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Forgive me. You tell us the time.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember well, it should have been somewhere in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Forgive me. Very well. Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I saw it on his desk, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did that come as a surprise?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I was really surprised indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: How did you feel about it, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I wondered how that thing ended up on his desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you feel that the presence of that -- did you feel that that list being put into Mr. Drljaca's hands was going to assist or hinder your preparation of Mr. Tadic's defence case at trial?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: At that moment, I had an answer to the question that crossed my mind earlier, why were people visited by the police not to contact me, not to speak to me, not to see me, who I never approached before, how come that exactly those people were approached? And that was the answer. He had the list. I remember a lawyer in Prijedor who had been approached by the police, and I was really flabbergasted that they picked this lawyer out to approach, that the person should not speak to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Forgive me: Who had picked this particular lawyer out to --

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, the lawyer was approached by the police, that the lawyer should not speak to me, not see me. The lawyer was very afraid to do so. So when the lawyer was contacted later on, we learned that. And I was really surprised. How come that they contacted that lawyer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: So for how long would you say, before you actually saw the list on the chief of police's desk in Prijedor police station, had you had this feeling that people you were trying to get hold of were already saying, "No, no, I don't want to see you"?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's very difficult to say. I can't put that in time. I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did it frustrate your attempts to obtain witnesses to support what Mr. Tadic had to say?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Paragraph 15, you say that you spoke to Mr. Vujin about the list and how it got onto Mr. Drljaca's desk, and you tell us that he admitted that it was he who gave that list to Mr. Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And sought to explain that he thought it would help in tracking down the witnesses. You say you regard that as downright absurd --

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- given that Mr. Vujin must have been as aware as you were, and probably more so, of Mr. Drljaca's attitude to your investigation. Can I put it this way: Did you believe Mr. Vujin's explanation as to why he said he gave that Defence witness list to Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It would be extremely naive, so I didn't view it in that way. I felt it was highly improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: It may be too obvious to ask, but did he, to your knowledge, ask you, Mr. Kay, or Mr. Orie, permission to do such a thing as that?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: If he had asked you, Mr. Orie, or Mr. Kay, for permission to do it, what would you have said?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No. But I would also have asked him why he was asking so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kay and Mr. Orie, what was their feeling when they learnt from you the news about this Defence witness list finding its way onto the chief of police's desk at Prijedor, pre-trial?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: They felt the same as I just expressed myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: How big an impact did that have on your Defence team?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I can only guess. It's very difficult to say, but as far as I experienced, it was more difficult to approach people who were on the list. And some of them never turned up or I couldn't find any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You mentioned a witness called "U," who was given the letter "U," who made certain admissions in relation to what had happened. Can you just expand that a little bit for us, please?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, that might be a little bit difficult. I have written, in fact, and later on, I thought I should have written, as far as I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I remember one witness, and I thought it was Witness U, who made the reference in evidence before the Trial Chamber about being harassed by the police, and I took it that that was an example of a witness who had been harassed by the police on the instruction of Mr. Drljaca, because he was aware that person was a potential witness. No one told me that the police were instructed by Mr. Drljaca, but I took it as an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. You deal with, at paragraph 16, with it being impossible to gauge how large an extent that interference with the witnesses had. You can tell us that you know it has an effect, but the speculation, I suppose, is to say how large it was. You'll never know the extent of it, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But the reason why I wrote it down was to show that there's a blank area here we can only speculate about, but it must have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And you say, "Without, therefore, being able to point to any particular witnesses with whom there was successful interference, I'm quite certain it happened and was probably widespread amongst the witnesses such as police officers, military officials, and civil servants who might have been in a position to give most assistance to me in my enquiries." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I feel it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You give an example, in paragraph 18, of some potential witnesses you were trying to track down?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Meakic, Mr. Milorad Tadic. Pausing there, that's not a relative of Mr. Tadic, is it, just a similar surname? And Mr. Milorad Danicic?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Meakic never showed up. Mr. Danicic was a person who was described to me as a lookalike of Mr. Dusko Tadic. And Mr. Milorad Tadic, the name, it's obvious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, are we perhaps straying a little from the main lines of the charges presented in the scheduling order?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm not going to go into this in too much detail. The reason I'm dealing with it is because I come back to what I said in my written submissions as to why Mr. Wladimiroff's evidence should be admitted. It goes very much to the question of Mr. Vujin's motive in these actions, and his motive can be gauged and assessed by the effect of his acts. I don't want to develop again the point I've made about the pattern of conduct in this case of behaving against one's own client's interest, of which the specific allegations, if this Chamber finds are proved, are examples. This background enables the Court to see those specific allegations in their context, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you then be good enough to treat the background with the limitations which are appropriate for background material?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed I will, and forgive me if I take too long on it. I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Let me deal with it this way,

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you consider those to be important people to speak to to try and run Mr. Tadic's defence to its best advantage?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, they were important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Were your efforts, after the witness list had been placed into Mr. Dracula's [sic] hands -- I'm sorry, I keep saying that. Drljaca's hands. Forgive me. Did you consider that your efforts to get hold of them were hindered?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you consider, in your experience, that the account that they gave you, when you finally managed to speak to them, those you could speak to, two out of the three, I believe -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you consider that they were giving you an honest and frank account of what they had to say?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not at all. I had a very strong feeling that they were well prepared and launched to show me that they were totally irrelevant, I was looking for the wrong persons, and I was stupid to ask for their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you get the feeling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, I'm not too certain of the connection between this and the charges presented against Mr. Vujin with which the Appeals Chamber is now concerned. This goes rather to the question as to whether the conviction was sound. We are concerned with certain allegations against Mr. Vujin to the effect that he deliberately manipulated certain evidence, to use the phrase which the witness has used. I think that's a good phrase, in the sense that that goes to the meat of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: If I can put it this way without repeating everything I just said, and it really is the last question on this particular topic and it's concentrating on the last sentence in paragraph 18, that the point is that once these witnesses' names have got into the other camp, if I can put it that way, once they had been put into the hands of the chief of police, that it's this witness's feeling not only did those witnesses lie but they appeared to be singing from the same hymn sheet, as if someone had coached them or choreographed, to use Mr. Wladimiroff's word, in what to say, and that may be very important because again it is against the interests of Mr. Tadic, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, would you kindly ask that last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Why did you feel that the evidence that they were giving you was carefully choreographed?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We asked verification questions, and they were able to produce immediately, at the spot, the documents to support that, each of them. I was really surprised they had all these documents ready at their pockets. It really struck me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Is that something you had encountered before in your interviewing other people before you got the list, that they were, as it were, ready and prepared with all the answers?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Some may have one document, but these people were extremely well prepared. That was totally obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. You then make a comment in the paragraph 19, and I ask you, without reference to it: As you came -- as the months went by and you came to see the full picture of what was going on, I ask you bluntly, did you trust Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I lost trust in him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: In whose interests, having worked alongside Mr. Vujin -- and I'm looking now at paragraph 24 -- having worked alongside with Mr. Vujin for the period of time that you tell us you did, in whose interests did Mr. Vujin appear, in reality, to be working?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sometimes I had this feeling that he was only working for himself, because as I told you at the very beginning, he popped up in the case. He was never assigned, but still he was there, making himself -- how do you say in English -- necessary. Later on, I changed that mind into trying to be helpful and naive, not very professional, and that changed it to someone who is taking control of the case for different aims. And I was leading the case, and that whole change of feelings added to a feeling of we should get rid of him because he's not taking care of the interests of Mr. Tadic; he is also taking care of someone else's interests. It might be the authorities, it might be other people, I don't know, but he is not the right person in this case, that we should get rid of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you consider he was working in the interests of his client, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sometimes he did, and as I wrote in the statement, then it coincided with other interests. But on many occasions later on, I felt this is very counter-productive, this is not in the interests of Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: When Mr. Tadic's own personal interests conflicted with the interests, if I can put it this way, of the State, the Serbian State, in whose interest did you assess Mr. Vujin was working in?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, I can only answer that question if I take into account what I've been told by Mr. Tadic later on, when, excuse the phrase, my team was sacked by Mr. Tadic. Then he told me that Vujin told him -- so this is really hearsay evidence -- that Vujin told him that if he would have the case, then Mr. Tadic would have the full cooperation of the authorities of the Republika Srpska, the right witnesses and the right documents; and that, in my feeling, was the right answer to how we looked at Mr. Vujin at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You say, towards the end of paragraph 24, "His interests," that is, Mr. Vujin's, "seems to me to have been to defend the Serb cause and to protect other people from becoming involved in Mr. Tadic's defence"?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's an observation that I made at the very end, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do you stand by that still?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have a very strong feeling that that is a right observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. We may hear, in due course, some evidence that Mr. Milan Vujin was very professionally, conscientiously, and expertly doing his work on the defence of Dusko Tadic. I just ask you this: Did you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It did not meet the standards I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a detail. You had interviewed various people during the course of your investigations. Were there examples of Mr. Vujin going to see those people and interviewing them after you or another member of your team had done so?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have no evidence of that, but again I've been told by the youngest brother, Ljubomir, of Mr. Tadic, that he travelled in the area at occasions when we were not there, which is very easy because we were only there on a few occasions, talking to people amongst whom also people we have been spoken to. Again, I'm terribly sorry, I can't give you any name or date because I simply don't remember, but that's what I've been told by the youngest brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Had you asked Mr. Vujin to go and see witnesses again after you or Mr. Kay or Mr. Orie had already interviewed them, that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, but if I'm fair, he could have understood that as all being in the game, being a member of the team in those days. But I gave no specific instructions whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well. I would just like to ask you this: The circumstances of Mr. Vujin's leaving the team, all right, just in a few words, did Mr. Vujin leave because he wanted to do another case or something like that, or what was it that caused him to leave the case?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, actually, it was Mr. Orie who did that. I was in the hospital in those days because I was ill in March and April '96. I had a herniated disc. As far as I remember well, there was also a story of Mr. Vujin taking another case, and we felt that the interests of that client -- I don't know the name -- might also be a potential conflict of interest with the case of Mr. Tadic. And then Mr. Orie, in one other way -- I've not been there, so I simply remember what I have been told -- told Mr. Vujin that we should separate, and he used that other case, as far as I remember, as an excuse to soften the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I see. So if it's put this way, he was tactfully told that he would be better to leave this case?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: The Tadic case?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I've been told, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I just want to show you, please, a letter. Would you see that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: There are some copies for Your Honours. Could you distribute those copies? Give that to the witness, and distribute those copies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will be Exhibit 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: This is a letter that's some time after the event, in English, it's an English translation, and in B/C/S at the back. Do you see it, Mr. Wladimiroff, I think signed by yourself?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: We see it's dated the 12th of May, '97?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: It's after the conviction, I think, at trial, 12th of May, '97. It's to Mr. Tadic's brother, Ljubo Tadic. What I particularly want to deal with: "Thank you for your fax. I'm very sorry that cooperation with Dusko has ceased, since" -- and I believe that "Steven" is inserted there in handwriting -- "Sylvia, and I did not want to cooperate with Vujin, and in view" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you slow down for the interpreters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Sorry. "I'm very sorry that cooperation with Dusko has ceased since Steven, Sylvia, and I did not want to cooperate with Vujin, and in view of the experience from the past, I do not need to explain why we think that."

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do you see where I am in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Is that first paragraph a reference to the difficulties which you, Mr. Kay, and Mr. Orie had experienced with working professionally with Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's a very short reflection of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: That's what that paragraph was dealing with?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You didn't wish to go into the detail, but --

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Certainly not write it down on an open fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You wanted to make clear where you all stood?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you want to stay in the case if Mr. Vujin was going to come back into it?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, that we made that clear to Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Is that because of the matters which you've been telling us about this morning --

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- and have put in your declaration?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: May I just ask you about this? Again, we heard a little bit of evidence about it. I think you gave an assessment to Ljubo that the case could have resulted, in the end, in a sentence of something like four to five years?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let me read that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Of course, right at the end, simply so that we know that that information was passed to Ljubo Tadic by way of a letter.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. The last thing I'd wish to do -- there are two more excerpts, Your Honours, from the video which we saw this morning, and the copy of a transcript that I have includes those two. I don't know whether Your Honours' transcript is the same, but it's the one that I understood to have been exhibited on the last occasion, two passages which relate to Mr. Wladimiroff speaking to a commentator. Do Your Honours have that? In the copy that I've been provided with by the Court, after the passage that we've just had translated, there's a passage that begins "002125".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We're a little handicapped here, Mr. Abell. We see the document to which you made reference earlier this morning in English and, I believe, in B/C/S also, and then there's a third page. That is a document headed -- I think it's the same thing. It's the same thing. It's all the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I believe that's dealing with the Dutch subtitles, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, as I say, this was provided by the Court, and it appears to be a segment of what was provided on the last occasion to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If you call it an exhibit number, perhaps the Registrar may be able to ferret it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Well, I believe it was given the number Exhibit 8A on the last occasion, when it was shown to Mr. Livingston. But because Mr. Livingston couldn't recognise the video, we never got to the other two passages. And I know, and I know Ms. Hollis knows, that there are two other passages which were translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can you locate that to us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two other excerpts of that same video cassette, videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could those be made available to the Bench and to the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will give you a copy of the excerpt. You mentioned that it was at 2125, Mr. Abell. It will be marked 39, and the excerpt of 252227 will be marked 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful, and may I say this is my last topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Do you think we might conveniently conclude with your last topic before the commencement of the coffee break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I hope so. This should be a matter of minutes, this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, would you like a copy of this to be provided to the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, please, and perhaps they can satisfy themselves that it is accurate whilst it's being played, and of course to Mr. Wladimiroff as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, as you can perhaps see when you are given the document, what we are dealing with is a couple of passages in the video where you are being interviewed by the commentator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We're in your hands, Mr. Abell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. Could, please, the video be played?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As we said earlier, the two transcripts that we have just distributed are not within or taken up within the cassette, the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was our understanding -- I see Ms. Hollis and I both looking puzzled -- that that was with the Court. It was our understanding that that cassette had both these segments on it as well. I have got a complete video, but it's not turned to the relevant portion, I'm afraid to say. Can I try and deal with it in this way, Your Honours? Can I try and deal with it in this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: You have in front of you, Mr. Wladimiroff, a translation?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. Two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Two of them. One of them is yourself speaking to an interviewer about Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, I see Mr. Domazet on his legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Perhaps we had better hear from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood well, Mr. Abell has the whole tape. As far as we know, it lasts some 20 minutes. We are in agreement with this, and we suggest that the entire tape be shown, of course including these two excerpts, but we think it might be good to see the entire tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Well, with respect, that's a matter for Mr. Domazet, if he wish to do that, but I'm really trying to deal with what appears to me to be relevant, bearing in mind this is a documentary. I'm not going to object if he wants to play the entire tape. I think it may be a little longer than 20 minutes, with respect, but there we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Domazet, you may have the tape played in its entirety during your case. At this stage, we suggest Mr. Abell should proceed in the way that he wishes. He is managing his case, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: May I just deal with it in this way,

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You can see there --

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could you give me the time portion? Because there are two documents here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, I was just going to: 00:21:25, and the first line is "Michael Wladimiroff: He says that he didn't do anything. "Interviewer: Do you believe that?" And you're being asked questions there about Mr. Tadic, obviously, aren't you? And then after that conversation -- firstly, do you remember having that conversation with the interviewer? I'm trying to get you to identify it, you see.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, but if I'm right in thinking, that portion was taken at the very beginning. It may have been somewhere in August or September or October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. And you -- yes. You there appear to be being asked the classic lawyer's question about -- "Well, what do you think?" And you're saying, "Well, my job is" -- you're effectively saying, "My job is, as a lawyer, not to let that clog up my work; I get on with defending"?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. And then over the page, at least on my copy it's over the page, the commentator says, "A month later, a peace agreement has been reached in Dayton" -- that's a reference, obviously, to the Dayton agreement; that would be December of '95 -- "A month later, a peace agreement has been reached in Dayton, but Wladimiroff has not made an inch of progress with his investigation. He is cross with his Yugoslav colleague, Vujin. He makes a secret flying visit to Karadzic, during which he does not want to take along a camera crew." Do you remember that part of the video as well?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: The commentary?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm not sure when that was written or thought of, but anyhow, it has been put together later on, somewhere by the second half -- perhaps even later; the first month of 1997. So I don't know when he made up that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well. Just this part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are you saying to the Court you remember saying these things, and in your recollection, these things should appear in the video to which reference has already been made? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, my position is that I can vouch for what I have said. As far as I'm quoted, I cannot vouch for the commentator. It's his impression of what he heard me saying over the months, over two years' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I appreciate that qualification, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this, that the statement "He's cross with his Yugoslav colleague, Vujin" -- not made directly by you, but made by the commentator -- does that broadly agree or disagree with your views about your colleague, Vujin?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have no doubt that I made it utterly clear to him that I was cross with Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the last passage should be Exhibit 40, 00:25:22 to 00:27:00. Do you have that, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, it appears to be the commentator first of all, and then yourself. "The Commentator: February '96, Wladimiroff has to go to Bosnia for a third time; as usual, via Belgrade. His colleague, Vujin, is not doing a good job." And then you're quoted: "It's becoming ever more awkward, because he is not keeping his promises, and we are increasingly getting worried about his role. This means that we are wondering whether he should still have a place in this team, because we are increasingly faced with the question of whether this is co-operation, or lack of co-operation, or even worse. Perhaps he is pursuing goals which we are not pursuing." Now, that's you, isn't it --

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- speaking on camera of Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said, "... lack of co-operation, or even worse. Perhaps he is pursuing goals which we are not pursuing"?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Actually, that's reflecting what I just told you, my development in mind, how to look at Vujin. And I think it reflects quite accurately that we could not exclude that he would have been counterproductive to the case, so we should get rid of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. In other words, not pursuing your goals of putting forward Mr. Tadic's defence in its best possible light?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And then the commentator speaks of your team operating in Banja Luka, and that being seriously sabotaged by the chief of police. Is that a reference to what you told us about the Defence witness list and the fallout, if I can put it that way, from that Defence witness list being put in the hands of Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have no doubt that I must have given him, the commentator, the impression of what he has said here on the basis of saying things I told you here, but more in details, because my memory was fresh at that date, on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And then we have a discussion between yourself and Mr. Orie, which I'm not going to read out, and the commentator referring to Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a little bit surprised to read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm really asking you about your comments there, and Mr. Orie's. Does that accord with your recollection of what you said on camera?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You refer to what I have said and what Mr. Orie --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What you and Mr. Orie have said.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Not the commentator. We understand you can't speak for him.

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I do remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. So although there's a little hiccup about the actual playing of the video, having seen the transcript of it, you are satisfied, Mr. Wladimiroff, that that's a transcript of what you had to say during that documentary about Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: JONKHEER MICHAIL WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. That portion that you referred to, myself speaking with Mr. Orie, was in Belgrade after we had spoken to Mr. Kostic, who was an investigator we retained.
